title: HPDT MLS17/393P — Ms C (Medical Laboratory Scientists and Technologists)
text:

DISCIPLINARY TRIUNAL
DECISION NO 922/MLS17/393P
the Health Practitioners Competence
Assurance Act 2003 (“the Act”)
of a disciplinary charge laid against a health
practitioner under Part 4 of the Act.
A PROFESSIONAL CONDUCT
COMMITTEE appointed by the
MEDICAL SCIENCES COUNCIL OF
NEW ZEALAND
Applicant
Ms C of X, registered medical laboratory
scientist
Practitioner
28 September 2017
and Ms P Rowe (Members in person)
Kendrick, and Mr C Sharma (Members by
Officer)
Professional Conduct Committee (PCC)
in person

Introduction
1. Ms C (“the practitioner”) is a registered medical laboratory scientist employed by the
Auckland District Health Board. She is a [ ].
2. On 7 July 2017, a Professional Conduct Committee appointed by the Medical Sciences
Council laid a disciplinary charge against the practitioner under the Health Practitioners
Competence Assurance Act 2003 (the HPCA Act).
3. The Notice of Charge alleges that, during the period 1 April 2016 to 19 March 2017,
the practitioner practised in her profession of medical laboratory science while not
holding a current practising certificate, in breach of section 100(1)(d) of the HPCA
Act.
4. The hearing proceeded on the basis of an Agreed Summary of Facts dated 31 August
2017 and an Agreed Bundle of Documents. The Agreed Bundle included the
practitioner’s registration information and correspondence between the Council and the
practitioner. The practitioner has accepted that she unintentionally practised without an
Annual Practising Certificate (“APC”) for the period of the charge. The Tribunal must
still determine whether the charge is established and if so what, if any, penalty should
apply.
5. This is the first hearing of the Tribunal to proceed using a video link conference
facility. This is a trial procedure adopted with the consent of both parties in this
proceeding. The aim of the trial is to determine if some one-day hearings, based on
agreed summaries of facts, might be more efficiently conducted with the use of video
link conferencing for the attendance of Tribunal Members or the parties. In this case,
three of the Tribunal Members residing out of Auckland attended the hearing by video
link. The remainder of the Tribunal and the parties were present at the hearing in
person in Auckland. The parties’ co-operation in this trial is acknowledged by the
Tribunal.
Legal principles in respect of the charge
6. The charge must be established on the balance of probabilities and the onus of proof
rests on the PCC.
7. The relevant provision section 100(1)(d) of the HPCA Act provides:
2

“100 Grounds on which health practitioner may be disciplined
(1) The Tribunal may make any 1 or more of the orders authorised by section 101
if, after conducting a hearing on a charge laid under section 91 against the
health practitioner, it makes 1 or more findings that - …
(d) the practitioner has practised his or her profession while not holding
a current practising certificate”
8. Under s100(1)(d) of the HPCA Act, the following three elements must be established:
(a) The practitioner was a registered medical laboratory scientist during the dates
set out in the charge;
(b) The practitioner practised as a medical laboratory scientist during the same
period; and
(c) The practitioner did not hold a current practising certificate during that period.
9. A charge does not require any intention to flout professional obligations or even that
the practitioner knew or ought to have known that she did not have a current APC.1
The offence of practising without a current practising certificate is an absolute offence
in this sense.
10. The current charge is to be distinguished from charges of misconduct under s100(1)(a)
and (b) of the HPCA Act, under which the Tribunal must be satisfied the offence is
sufficiently serious to justify disciplinary sanction.2 In the present case, the Tribunal
must simply determine if the three elements of the charge set out s100(1)(d) of the Act
are established.
Facts
11. The Tribunal is satisfied the following relevant facts are established.
12. Since April 2009, the practitioner has been registered as a medical laboratory scientist,
practising in the area of [ ]. She has worked part-time as a medical laboratory scientist
since 2006.
1 Dr E (503/Den/12/219P) at [76], White (366/Opt10/168P) at [9], Henderson (477/Phar12/210P and
Phar12/213P) at [36], Ms H (256/Psy09/128P) at [6] and [7], Bhatia (344/Med10/151P) at [74].
2 Dr E (503/Den/12/219P) at [39] to [43]; Ms R (689/MLS14/294P) at [9]-[18].
3

13. Prior to 1 April 2017, the practitioner held and renewed her APC for seven consecutive
years from 2009 to 2016 (from 1 April to 31 March each year). However, the
practitioner did not apply for an APC for the 2016/2017 practising year, which
commenced on 1 April 2016. The practitioner has admitted this.
14. In April 2016, the Medical Sciences Council (“Council”) sent the practitioner an email
recording that her APC had expired and that, if she intended to continue practising, she
needed to apply for an APC immediately. The email was sent to the email address held
by the Council for the practitioner. However, that email address was later discovered
to be obsolete and the email was never received by the practitioner. The practitioner
had not advised the Council that email address was obsolete and the Council did not
contact the practitioner again to remind her to renew her APC.
15. Despite not renewing her APC for the 2016/2017 practising year, the practitioner
continued to work for 16 hours per week as a [ ] with the ADHB between 1 April 2016
and 19 March 2017. The practitioner has admitted she did not hold an APC for that
period.
16. In March 2017, the practitioner applied for an APC for the 2017/2018 practising year
due to commence on 1 April 2017. In her application, she declared she had been
practising as a medical laboratory scientist for the previous 3 years. This triggered
enquires from the Council regarding the practitioner’s failure to hold an APC for the
2016/2017 practising year, which culminated in the Charge now before the Tribunal.
17. Later in March 2017, the practitioner obtained an APC for the remainder of the
2016/2017 year. The practitioner also obtained an APC for the 2017/2018 year. The
practitioner has held a current APC from 20 March 2017 onwards.
Finding on the charge
18. The Tribunal is satisfied that the three elements of the Charge under s100(1)(d) of the
Act are established. In particular:
(a) The practitioner was at all relevant times a registered medical laboratory
scientist;
(b) During the period of the charge, 1 April 2016 to 19 March 2017, she practised
as such while working at the Practice; and
4

(c) During the same period of the charge, the practitioner did not hold a current
APC.
Penalty
19. Given that the Tribunal is satisfied the charge is established, it must go on to
consider the appropriate penalty under s101 of the HPCA Act. The penalties may
include:
(a) Cancellation of registration;
(b) Suspension of registration for a period not exceeding 3 years;
(c) An order that the practitioner may only practise with conditions imposed on
employment or supervision or otherwise;
(d) Censure;
(e) A fine of up to $30,000; and
(f) An order as to costs of the Tribunal and/or the PCC to be met in part or in
whole by the practitioner.
20. The Tribunal accepts as the appropriate sentencing principles those contained in
Roberts v Professional Conduct Committee3 where Collins J identified the
following eight factors as relevant whenever the Tribunal is determining an
appropriate penalty. In particular the Tribunal is bound to consider what penalty:
(a) most appropriately protects the public and deters others;
(b) facilitates the Tribunal’s important role in setting professional standards;
(c) punishes the practitioner;
(d) allows for the rehabilitation of the health practitioner;
(e) promotes consistency with penalties in similar cases;
(f) reflects the seriousness of the misconduct;
3 [2012] NZHC 3354 at [44]-[51].
5

(g) is the least restrictive penalty appropriate in the circumstances; and
(h) looked at overall, is the penalty which is “fair, reasonable and
proportionate in the circumstances”.
21. The PCC seeks a penalty against the practitioner of censure, a fine of $1,000
together with costs.
22. The Tribunal was referred to a number of previous Tribunal cases in which
practitioners had inadvertently failed to renew their APC, but continued to practise
in breach of the Act.4 Those cases demonstrate the penalties imposed are
predominantly censure, together with a fine and contribution to costs. Fines have
tended to range from $1,000 to $2,500.
23. The Tribunal is satisfied that this case is most comparable with that in Ms R,5
determined in respect of another Medical Laboratory Scientist. In that case the
practitioner was held to have practised without a practising certificate for 18
months. The failure to renew the APC had occurred unintentionally, as a result of a
parental leave absence and return to work. The penalty imposed was censure and a
fine of $1,000 together with costs payable by the practitioner of $5,000.
Aggravating and Mitigating Factors
24. The Tribunal considers the only material aggravating factor in the present case is
that the practitioner practised without an APC for just under 12 months in total.
25. There are a number of mitigating factors:
(a) The practitioner has admitted her offending, apologised for her omission
and taken immediate steps to remedy the situation, including applying for
an APC.
(b) The offending was not deliberate. In correspondence between the Council
and PCC, the practitioner explained her failure to renew her APC was due
to a misunderstanding concerning the renewal process, and an honest belief
that her APC had been renewed.
4 Dr S (445/Den11/198P), Henderson (477/Phar12/210P), Ms H – (256/Psy09/128P), Williams
(632/Pod13/217P), Ms R (689/MLS14/294P).
5 Ms R (689/MLS14/294P)
6

(c) The practitioner had a particularly distracting and distressing period during
2016, with the ill-health and death of her mother.
(d) The offending did not involve any deception or deliberate action in ignoring
the renewal reminder sent.
(e) This is the practitioner’s first offence.
(f) There is no issue as to the practitioner’s competence.
(g) The offending did not cause any direct risk to public safety.
(h) The practitioner is unlikely to reoffend, given her previous history of
compliance.
Finding on Penalty
26. The APC is an important part of the regulatory regime. There are a number of
sections in the HPCA Act dealing with practitioners’ obligations in respect of the
APC. The importance of this obligation is underscored by the ground of discipline
provided by section 100(1)(d) of the Act.
27. The Tribunal accepts the practitioner’s failure to renew the APC was a breach of an
important professional obligation. While the breach was inadvertent, the
practitioner could have been more proactive in ensuring she had completed the
renewal process. Prior to 1 April 2016, she had applied for and held APCs for
seven practising years. The practitioner appears to have (incorrectly) believed the
APC application process had changed for the 2016/2017 practising year and that her
employer was to complete the APC process on her behalf. The Tribunal notes that
it is the practitioner’s primary responsibility to ensure she has a current APC under
the Act and this cannot be delegated. While the practitioner’s offending is certainly
at the lower end of the scale, it was over a period of almost 12 months which must
warrant some penalty.
28. The Tribunal does take the opportunity to note that other than the one Council email
of April 2017, there was no evidence that the Council made any other attempt to
7

contact the practitioner or verify that the APC renewal notice had reached the
practitioner. This is somewhat surprising given the consequences for practitioners.
It is our recommendation that the Council consider adopting a second line of follow
up to ensure that the renewal notice is received.
29. The Tribunal was also presented in evidence with a copy of the ADHB’s Annual
Practising Certificate Policy and Procedure (updated December 2004). This
provides that it is the ADHB’s responsibility to ensure that employee practitioners
hold a current APC. This includes a requirement that Line Managers sight each
staff member’s new APC before the current APC expires. However, we do note
that the ADHB policy appears not to have identified this matter. The practitioner’s
evidence was that the ADHB never raised the matter with her during the period she
was without an APC in 2016/2017. There is no other evidence before the Tribunal
as to whether the proper systems were in place and whether the practitioner’s failure
to renew her APC was followed up by the ADHB. The Tribunal is therefore
reluctant to make any criticism of the ADHB, but it is recommended that the
Council may wish to take the opportunity to raise this matter with the ADHB.
30. The Tribunal has taken into account the relevant sentencing principles, aggravating
and mitigating factors and the comparative cases. The Tribunal is of the view that
the appropriate penalty in this case is to include:
(a) A censure of the practitioner. The Tribunal must emphasise the importance
of the APC regime, with the associated professional obligations that fall on
each individual practitioner. The Tribunal therefore orders censure to
express its disapproval for the omission which occurred in this case; and
(b) A fine to be paid by the practitioner of $1,000. This fine is set having
regard to the period over which the APC obligations were breached and is
consistent with similar cases in the range.
Costs
31. It is usual for an award of costs to be made against a practitioner once a charge is
established. In considering the appropriate quantum of costs, the Tribunal must
take into account the need for the practitioner to make a proper contribution towards
the costs. The Tribunal uses 50% of the total reasonable costs of the proceeding as
a starting point, in accordance with the dicta in Cooray v Preliminary Proceedings
8

Committee (Doogue J, HC Wellington, AP 23/94, 14 September 1995). The
Tribunal recognises that the practitioner has cooperated at all stages of the PCC’s
investigation and this prosecution.
32. The PCC’s costs were $15,921.23 and the Tribunal’s estimated costs are assessed as
$12,517.00, excluding GST.6
33. The practitioner produced evidence that her net income per week from her role with
the ADHB is $504.30. No further evidence as to her financial position was
provided.
34. Taking all factors into account, the Tribunal orders the practitioner pay 20% of the
total costs incurred, to be paid as follows:
(a) A contribution to the PCC’s costs of $3,184
(b) A contribution towards the Tribunal’s costs of $2,503.
Publication of Name
35. The practitioner currently has interim name suppression, and has applied for
permanent suppression of her name and identifying details. The application is
based on the grounds that:
(a) The practitioner’s career has thus far been unblemished. This is her first
disciplinary matter before the Tribunal;
(b) Publication would have a disproportionate impact on her reputation and
career given the low-level offending;
(c) Her offending is at the lower end of the scale in terms of seriousness;
(d) There is a risk of undue distress and anxiety being caused to current and
past patients of ADHB if suppression orders are not made, given the area of
specialist practice the practitioner works in which involves vulnerable
6 The Tribunal’s written estimated costs schedule produced at hearing was for $13,517. However, the
Chair’s post hearing costs were reduced at hearing by $1,000 given the reduced time needed to
produce this decision.
9

patients. It is submitted that patients may incorrectly consider this Charge
reflects adversely on the practitioner’s clinical competence which it does
not; and
(e) There is no public interest in publication as there are no public safety or
professional competence matters arising in this case.
36. The practitioner’s application was not opposed by the PCC.
37. Section 95 of the Act requires every hearing of the Tribunal to be in public, but also
provides the Tribunal with the discretion to make non-publication orders if it is
“desirable” to do so. The exercise of the discretion involves weighing the
competing public and private interests. This includes the interests of the public in
transparency and freedom of reporting of the disciplinary process and in knowing
the name of health practitioners subject to disciplinary proceedings.7 As against
these interests, there are the private interests of the practitioner and others that may
be adversely impacted if suppression is not granted.
38. The Tribunal considers it is desirable in this case to permanently suppress the names
of the practitioner and the Practice, for the following reasons:
(a) The practitioner has raised the point that she deals with emotional and
vulnerable clients who may place disproportionate weight on the
practitioner’s offending and wrongly associate it with her competency. The
Tribunal accepts there is a genuine risk of this nature to the practitioner’s
career and reputation.
(b) The practitioner’s name is unusual and may adversely affect her son, whom
the practitioner advises is considering a career in medicine.
(c) Publication is also likely to have an adverse effect on the Practice, which
serves a number of private patients.
(d) The likely adverse effects on the practitioner and the Practice are
disproportionate to the public interest, given the lack of any public safety
concerns arising.
7 A useful summary of the competing interests has been provided by the High Court in Anderson v
PCC HC Wellington, CIV 2008-485-1646, 14 November 2008.
10

Conclusion
39. The charge under section 100(1)(d) of the HPCA Act is made out.
40. The penalty orders made against the practitioner by this Tribunal are as follows:
(a) Censure;
(b) A fine of $1,000 to be paid by the practitioner;
41. Costs are to be paid by the practitioner of $5,687; apportioned $3,182 payable to the
PCC and $2,503 payable to the Tribunal.
42. The practitioner is granted permanent name suppression, under s95 of the HPCA
Act, including suppression of any identifying features which will include the name
of the Practice and her role as a [ ].
43. Subject to the Tribunal’s suppression orders above, the Tribunal directs that a copy
of this decision and a summary be published on the Tribunal’s website. The
Tribunal also requests the Medical Sciences Council to publish either a summary of,
or a reference to, the Tribunal’s decision in its principal professional publications to
members, in either case including a reference to the Tribunal’s website so as to
enable interested parties to access the decision.
DATED at Auckland this 30th day of October 2017
................................................................
MJ Dew
Chairperson
Health Practitioners Disciplinary Tribunal
